To expurgate something means to deliberately remove parts of a written work — a book, a script, a song, a speech, a letter, or any similar material — because those parts are considered offensive, indecent, immoral, politically dangerous, or otherwise unfit for a particular audience.

Think of it this way: imagine someone takes a novel and goes through it with scissors, cutting out every scene they find too violent, too sexual, or too controversial. What remains is a "cleaned up" version. That act of cutting — that deliberate removal of objectionable content from a text — is expurgation.
What makes this different from regular editing?

This is crucial. Ordinary editing is about improving a piece of writing — fixing errors, tightening sentences, restructuring ideas. Expurgating is something more specific and more loaded. It is about removing content purely on moral, religious, political, or social grounds. The goal is not to make the writing better; the goal is to make it more acceptable — usually to a particular authority, institution, or audience.
What kinds of things get expurgated?

Almost anything that someone in a position of power considers inappropriate. Profanity, sexually explicit scenes, violent passages, blasphemous ideas, politically subversive arguments, racial slurs — all of these have historically been expurgated from texts at one time or another.

For example, a government might expurgate a novel before allowing it to be published, removing paragraphs that criticize the ruling party. A religious body might expurgate a manuscript, cutting out passages it considers heretical. A publisher preparing a book for children might expurgate all the adult language and mature content from a classic novel. A school board might expurgate chapters from a history textbook it finds controversial.

In every case, the process is the same: identify the objectionable material, remove it, and present the remaining content as the "approved" version.

The word almost always applies to texts and recorded material.

Expurgate lives most naturally in the world of books, manuscripts, scripts, films, recordings, and speeches. You expurgate a text or something that can be read, heard, or watched. You would not typically say you expurgated a painting or a physical object. The word is at home in discussions of publishing, literature, censorship, film, and history.
The tone and connotation of the word

This is important: expurgate is not a neutral word. It carries a subtle but clear negative charge. When you say a book has been expurgated, the implication is that something has been lost — that the original work has been damaged, diluted, or dishonestly presented. The word quietly suggests that the act of removal was presumptuous, heavy-handed, or even dishonest.

Compare the "expurgated edition" of a book with the "complete edition" or the "unexpurgated edition" — the very existence of these labels tells you that readers generally view the expurgated version as inferior, as a compromised version of the real thing.

This is why expurgate is often used with a critical or disapproving tone. When a writer says their work was expurgated by a publisher, they're not usually pleased about it.
How it relates to similar words — and how it differs

Censor is the broadest of these words. It refers generally to suppressing, blocking, or controlling material — not just in texts, but in media, speech, and public life. Expurgate is narrower: it's specifically about the act of removing objectionable content from within a text, not blocking the whole thing.

Bowdlerize means almost the same thing as expurgate, but it specifically implies excessive, overly prudish, or ridiculous removal — the kind that strips a classic work of its power or soul. It's stronger in its mockery. Expurgate is the serious, formal term; bowdlerize is the slightly contemptuous one.

Sanitize is more general — you can sanitize information, a story, a reputation, a message. Expurgate is specifically about cutting material out of a text on grounds of moral or social objection.

Redact is about blacking out specific information in official documents — usually for legal, governmental, or security reasons. You redact a name from a court document. The motivation for redaction is confidentiality, not morality. Expurgation is motivated by moral or social judgment.

"The publisher decided to expurgate several chapters of the novel before releasing it for the school market."

"Critics were outraged that the film had been expurgated so heavily that entire storylines had disappeared."

"The authoritarian regime expurgated all references to the uprising from the official history textbooks."

"Scholars prefer to read the unexpurgated version of the diary, since the expurgated version hides some of the most revealing entries."
When would you use this word?

Expurgate is a formal, educated word. You would use it in writing about literature, censorship, publishing history, politics, or media. You would not use it in casual conversation — it would sound stiff and out of place. But in an essay, a review, a critical article, or an academic discussion, it is precise and powerful.

To expurgate is to remove passages or content from a text that someone has judged offensive, inappropriate, or dangerous — producing a cleaned-up version that is typically seen as a lesser, compromised form of the original.
